conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’m so glad we have a few minutes to talk while you’re feeding your little one.  

I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally during the first weeks and months after birth. There’s no pass or fail; it just gives us a snapshot so we can offer the right support.  

Everything you share is confidential within our care team, and you can take a break or skip anything you’re not comfortable answering. When we’re done, we’ll go over how things look and decide together what might be helpful next.  

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:  

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[shifts the baby a little higher on my lap, eyes still on her face]

Um… definitely not as much as I used to. I’ll smile when she makes those little milk-drunk faces, but actually laughing—maybe once or twice the whole week. My husband tried to joke about the diaper explosions and I just couldn’t get there. I mostly feel… flat, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[keeps my voice low so I don’t startle the baby]

Honestly… no, not really. I can smile at her tiny yawns, but a real laugh feels kind of impossible right now. My sister sent me a funny video and I just stared at it, felt nothing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[bounces the baby gently]

Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but lately even that feels like one more chore. I still go, because I know it’s good for me, but the “looking-forward” part isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to the baby’s head, voice soft]

Yeah… a couple of times. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—like if I were a better mom I’d know the “trick” to settle her. Rationally I know babies just have rough days, but the voice in my head still says, “You should have figured it out by now.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[rubs the baby’s back, voice tight]

Mostly at night, once the house gets quiet. I’ll lie there listening to her breathe and suddenly my chest feels tight—what if she stops? What if I miss something? I know the pediatrician said she’s healthy, but I still check her every ten minutes. No real reason, just… scared.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[rocking the baby a little faster]

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. Like yesterday in the grocery line—suddenly my heart was racing, I felt hot, and I had to leave the cart and go sit in the car. Nothing was wrong, but for a minute I thought I might pass out. It passed, but it left me shaky the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath, eyes still on the baby]

Yes… most days. It’s like every small task—folding a basket of laundry, answering one text—feels ten times heavier. I’ll start something, then she fusses and I think, “I can’t keep up.” I’m not falling apart, but it’s like I’m always one step behind and the pile just keeps growing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[strokes baby’s cheek, voice quiet]

A few nights this week. I’ll finally get her down, but then my mind keeps spinning—did I burp her long enough, is the swaddle too tight, what if she wakes up the second I close my eyes? I lie there wired, checking the monitor every few minutes. I wouldn’t say I’m miserable-miserable, just… restless and heavy, like I can’t turn the worry off long enough to drift off.
I have felt sad or miserable

[keeps gaze on the baby, voice low]

Yeah… it comes in waves. I’ll be fine while I’m busy with her, then suddenly feel this wash of sadness—like yesterday, just looking out the window at the rain. I teared up for no real reason. It’s not every minute, but it’s definitely there, hovering.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, eyes still on the baby]

Not really… I’ve felt teary, but actual crying—maybe once this week. It was the middle of the night, she wouldn’t latch, and I just felt this lump in my throat. A couple tears slipped out, but I wiped them fast and kept going. Mostly I’m just kind of numb and tired, not sitting here sobbing or anything.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, pulling the baby a little closer]

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can take care of her.

You've shared how the joy that used to come easily-laughing at a video, looking forward to coffee-now feels distant, replaced by <sym>anhedonia</sym>, waves of <sym>sadness</sym>, and nights of checking your baby every ten minutes because <sym>anxiety</sym> grips your chest. You're working hard to stay afloat, yet even small tasks feel ten times heavier, and a panic attack in the grocery line left you shaky all day. Still, you're clear that self-harm is not on your mind and your love for your daughter shines through every answer.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient states a real laugh feels impossible and felt nothing at a funny video, clearly matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a couple of times" with specific example of feeling responsible for baby's nap trouble, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive nighttime worries with physical tension and compulsive checking despite reassurance, indicating very often experiencing anxiety without cause.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a classic unexpected panic attack (racing heart, heat, fear of fainting, lingering shakiness) that meets "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>She reports that most days feel overwhelming and she struggles to keep up, matching "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Her description of lying awake with racing worries most nights this week aligns with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent, noticeable sadness that intrudes unpredictably, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 21 exceeds the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. She endorses core symptoms: daily <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>laugh feels impossible</quote>), <sym>low mood</sym> (<quote>wash of sadness</quote>), <sym>self-blame</sym> (<quote>better mom would know the trick</quote>), physiologic <sym>anxiety</sym> with compulsive checking, two <sym>panic attacks</sym>, and functional impairment (<quote>one step behind</quote>). No suicidal ideation (Q10=0). EPDS 21 places her in the urgent-referral category per current guidelines. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within one week
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Encourage 15-min daytime rest while baby sleeps; practice 4-7-8 breathing when racing thoughts arise
4. Limit overnight monitor-checking to once unless medically indicated; invite partner to handle one nighttime resettle
5. Schedule EPDS re-screen in two weeks to track progress
6. Provide 24-h crisis line numbers and local <med>postpartum support group</med> contacts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report plus behavioral observations; 2–3 wks post-delivery.

Symptoms endorsed (≥ several days / most days):
- Marked anhedonia – minimal laughter, anticipatory enjoyment absent  
- Persistent low mood / tearfulness (“comes in waves”)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Nocturnal & generalized anxiety, intrusive “what-if” cognitions  
- Two panic-equivalent episodes (grocery, home) with physical symptoms  
- Overwhelm / reduced coping (“everything feels 10× heavier”)  
- Initial insomnia after night feeds linked to rumination  
- Crying episode once this week; otherwise “numb and tired”

Denies:
- Active suicidal ideation, intent, or plan  
- Thoughts of harming infant or self

Observed:
- Appropriate maternal vigilance; rapid soothing of infant; no psychomotor retardation  
- Affect congruent with reported mood; no psychotic content

Screening significance:
Meets provisional cutoff concern for Major Depressive Episode with anxious distress; also consistent with postpartum anxiety. No safety red-flags (self-harm), but distress and functional impairment warrant prompt follow-up evaluation for diagnosis and level-of-care determination.

Next step: Schedule within one week for comprehensive assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, clinical interview, supports review).
